title: AI for NONMEM Coding in Pharmacometrics Research and Education: Shortcut or Pitfall?

content.abstract_summary: Most comprehensive evaluation to date of LLMs for NONMEM coding in pharmacometrics: 7 LLMs tested (including OpenAI o1 and gpt-4.1) on 13 pharmacometrics tasks spanning a range of population PK and PD models. Developed a standardized scoring rubric for code accuracy assessment and created an optimized prompt. o1 and gpt-4.1 achieved 'great accuracy for all tasks when using our optimized prompt.' User review still essential for complex models. Discusses AI in pharmacometrics education and overreliance prevention. UNC Chapel Hill (CS + Pharmacy) + Monash Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences (Kirkpatrick, Landersdorfer). CPT:PSP 2025.
key_findings: 7 LLMs evaluated on 13 NONMEM tasks — most comprehensive pharmacometrics LLM benchmark to date; tasks span basic structural PK/PD models to complex population models

OpenAI o1 and gpt-4.1 achieved best performance, generating 'codes with great accuracy for all tasks when using our optimized prompt' — substantial improvement over shin_2024_llm (ChatGPT 4.0/Gemini, which still required expert correction)
Standardized scoring rubric developed for assessing NONMEM code accuracy — provides a reusable benchmark methodology for future LLM comparisons in pharmacometrics
Optimized prompt development: prompt engineering substantially improved LLM performance — suggests that raw LLM capability is not the only variable; prompt strategy matters as much as model choice
LLMs performed well for basic NONMEM structures; 'user review and refinement remain essential, especially for complex models with special dataset alignment or advanced coding techniques'

Education dimension: discusses preventing overreliance on AI for pharmacometrics coding — frames LLMs as scaffolding tools in educational settings, with attention to learning risks from uncritical adoption
limitations: Full text not yet read — abstract_only; PMC12706393 available for upgrade
Task set of 13 may not cover all complex NONMEM use cases (e.g., SAEM estimation, complex covariates, M3 method for BLQ, time-varying covariates)
Scoring rubric is new — not validated against expert review panels or clinical impact criteria
Does not evaluate LLMs for model interpretation, diagnostics, or simulation — only code generation

extracted_claims.text: The OpenAI o1 and gpt-4.1 models achieved the best performance, both generating codes with great accuracy for all tasks when using our optimized prompt.

Overall, LLMs performed well in writing basic NONMEM model structures, providing a useful foundation for pharmacometrics model coding. However, user review and refinement remain essential, especially for complex models with special dataset alignment or advanced coding techniques.

This work provides a benchmark for current LLMs' performance in NONMEM coding and introduces a practical prompt that can facilitate more accurate and efficient use of AI in pharmacometrics research and education.

numerical_findings.description: Number of NONMEM pharmacometrics tasks in benchmark

gaps_addressed: Updates and substantially supersedes shin_2024_llm for M4.4: shows that newer LLMs (o1, gpt-4.1) with prompt engineering achieve near-perfect NONMEM code accuracy — the capability gap documented by shin_2024_llm has largely closed for standard tasks
Prompt engineering as a pharmacometrics skill: optimized prompt development is a concrete, actionable WG recommendation — provides scaffolding the WG could publish or distribute to members
Education framing: LLMs as tools in pharmacometrics training, including overreliance prevention — relevant to WG's community-building role beyond research
Benchmark methodology: standardized scoring rubric is reusable infrastructure the WG could build on for future LLM comparisons

provenance.notes: Found via PubMed search 'GPT artificial intelligence pharmacokinetics population model pharmacometrics' (PMID 41187068). Full text available from PMC12706393 (DOI: 10.1002/psp4.70125). CPT:PSP 2025, 14(12):1965-1969. Open access. Zheng W + Yao H = UNC CS; Wang W + Zhou J = UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy; Kirkpatrick CMJ + Landersdorfer CB = Monash MIPS. Key contrast with shin_2024_llm: shin used 2 LLMs, 2 tasks, 2024; zheng uses 7 LLMs, 13 tasks, 2025 — and finds o1/gpt-4.1 with optimized prompts now achieve near-perfect accuracy. The pharmacometrics LLM capability trajectory has been steep. Update when upgraded to full_text.
